title: Dentistry — Advice letter to a parent: after a child's dental trauma
before:
WESTERGATE DENTAL PRACTICE
Patient: Thomas Van Rooyen-Obi, aged 9
Attended: 4 March 2029, emergency appointment at 16:30
Letter written: 4 March 2029

The injury:
Fell from a scooter at approximately 15:20, landing face first on a paved path. Wearing no helmet.
No loss of consciousness. No vomiting. No headache. No bleeding from the nose or ears.
He was seen by the school first aider, then brought straight here by his mother.
He has been reviewed for head injury by the practice and has no features requiring hospital
assessment; his mother has been given written head injury advice separately.

Dental findings:
Upper right central incisor: displaced palatally by approximately 4 mm, mobile, tender to touch.
Upper left central incisor: enamel-dentine fracture of the incisal edge, approximately 3 mm of
tissue lost, no pulp exposure, sensitive to air.
Both are permanent teeth with incomplete root formation, which is favourable for healing.
Lower lip: a 12 mm laceration on the inner surface, cleaned, no foreign body seen, not requiring
sutures.
No other tooth affected. No jaw fracture; the bite meets normally and there is no step in the arch.
No tooth fragment unaccounted for — the fractured piece was found at the scene and brought in.

Treatment carried out today:
Upper right central incisor repositioned under local anaesthetic and splinted to the adjacent teeth
with a flexible splint. The splint must stay in place for FOUR weeks.
Upper left central incisor: the fractured piece was reattached and the edge smoothed.
Radiographs taken: no root fracture, no alveolar fracture.
Sensibility testing carried out today for baseline: both teeth responded, and this has been recorded
so that any change at review can be recognised.
Tetanus status checked with his mother: up to date.

Aftercare that must be followed:
Soft diet for two weeks. Nothing that must be bitten with the front teeth — no apples, no crusty
bread, no corn on the cob. Food should be cut up and chewed at the back.
No sport of any kind, and no scooter or bicycle, until after the splint is removed and he has been
reviewed.
Cleaning is more important than usual, not less: a soft brush around the splint after every meal,
and a 0.12% chlorhexidine mouthrinse on a cotton bud applied along the gumline twice daily for two
weeks — he should not swish and swallow it.
Paracetamol at the correct dose for his weight for the first two or three days; the dose has been
written down. Ibuprofen may also be used and there is no reason to avoid it here.
The lip laceration will be sore for several days; it should be kept clean and he should avoid biting
it while it is numb, which is the commonest cause of a second injury on the day.

Appointments already booked:
11 March — one-week check.
1 April — splint removal at four weeks.
6 May, 4 August and 4 March 2030 — reviews with radiographs and sensibility testing at each.
These reviews continue for at least a year because problems can appear months after the injury.

What to watch for and report before the next appointment:
The tooth becoming darker or greyer in colour.
Pain that comes on by itself rather than only when touched.
A spot or swelling on the gum above the tooth.
The tooth becoming loose again, or the splint coming away.
Any swelling of the face, or fever.

What was explained today:
That the front tooth may still lose its nerve despite everything going well, and that this is not a
sign that anything has been done wrongly; it is why the reviews continue for a year.
That the reattached piece may need replacing with a filling later.
That a mouthguard is strongly advised for any contact sport once he is playing again, and that this
practice can make one.
His mother asked whether the teeth will "look normal again" and was told that the appearance can be
restored but that the long-term outlook depends on the reviews.
